utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. I can follow, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a chair. Appearances, Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner; Nicholas Koumjian; Anna Richterova, hidden; and Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning. Appearances, Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here this morning with Barbara Baruch and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. And welcome back, Ms. Baruch. Before I ask if you have any preliminaries I promised you a decision yesterday on the 24th motion for protective measures, which was filed by the Prosecution on the 4th of this month, of July. I will deal first with witness to whom the pseudonym BT105 is being suggested. The Prosecution has asked for pseudonym and image distortion by way of protective measures for this witness. The Chamber has seen the reasons put forward by the Prosecution as a ground for their request for these protective measures. The Trial Chamber agrees with them. Consequently, the protective measures requested are being granted effective immediately because I think this witness is coming over this morning, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, he's the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So then we have another witness for whom protective measures, consisting of pseudonym and closed session have been requested. It's been suggested that this witness, if granted a pseudonym, will be known as witness BT93. The Chamber has taken into consideration the reasons put forward by the Prosecution as ground for their request. For the time being the Chamber agrees to grant the protective measures requested, namely that of pseudonym and closed session, but wants to make it clear that it will interview the witness in the beginning of his testimony to confirm whether to continue with closed session -- in closed session or not. For the time being, the protective measures requested are being granted as requested. Therefore, the evidence of -- testimony of this witness will be referred to as BT93 will be heard in closed session. Any preliminaries, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's what's known as the jinx. If you want to finish a case quickly, something is always going to happen. Can I assure Your Honour that neither Mr. Ackerman nor myself were driving motor cars last night, but tomorrow's witness was in a car accident yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me -- he?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. He's in hospital. We had a phone call this morning from his secretary. He's in hospital with a broken arm and possible internal injuries and they are doing tests today. Your Honour, the trouble -- obviously he's in no fit state to testify tomorrow and he is committed to go abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On Saturday morning and it's unlikely he'll be fit to come here before that and certainly not to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where did the accident take place? Here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't tell Your Honour that -- I mean, I can but I will have to do it in private session, if we go into private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I do apologise to you. Please can you start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With regard to the issue with the Treasury Department and the fact that all of us from the United States are appearing here without a licence from the treasury, I want to report what happened yesterday. First of all, you're aware of the letter that was received by Ms. Sinatra, which basically said: Applying for a licence does not relieve you of your obligations to follow the law. Plus a previous letter to Mr. Hayman saying that: Appearing without a licence is in violation of a law, plus a conversation that I had with an officer at the Treasury Department saying that the letter, the authorisation letter is not a licence and that at best it's a defence if we are charged with some kind of an offence. Everyone now agrees with that proposition. We talked yesterday, as a result of this letter that we received yesterday, with Mr. Kay, who is a legal officer at the United States Embassy and is actively working on this matter. He told us that a general licence was supposed to have been issued last week, they thought they would have it last Thursday, and then some -- the general licence wound up on someone's desk in Washington, who became concerned about its rather broad language, and that delayed it. He now expects that it will be issued -- that we will have it tomorrow, this Wednesday. We told him that we were very reluctant because each day we appear in court is technically a felony violation of the United States code, that we were very reluctant to go forward after Wednesday if that licence is not issued. He informed us that that could be helpful to take that position because that would enable him to put some additional pressure on the Treasury Department to get it issued. So for purposes of the record today, Ms. Baruch and I are taking the position that we cannot appear in court after tomorrow unless we have a licence because we cannot continue to risk the violation of these regulations and a felony prosecution. That is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you suggest that this can be communicated to the legal officer in your embassy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was communicated to him yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. No. Your public statement of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can call him but he was -- it was made clear to him yesterday that this is the position we would take, I believe. Ms. Baruch agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I am doing is that, as I did on previous occasions, I'm asking the Registrar to block this part of the proceedings of today, copy it for President Meron, including the statement that I am going to make now, namely that I think at this point in time, it is important for this Tribunal to communicate to the officer mentioned by Mr. Ackerman, officer in the U.S. Embassy here in The Hague, the predicament that this Trial Chamber in particular would find itself in if -- starting from Thursday it will be unable to sit due to Mr. Ackerman not -- Mr. Brdjanin not being represented according to his rights. So that goes to President Meron, this morning, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as soon as I complete the cross-examination of the current witness, I'm going to ask your permission to depart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I will be immediately in touch with Larry Johnson at the President's office, and I'm confident that this matter will be worked out by Wednesday and I don't think it's going to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, Mr. Ackerman, because frankly the last week or so, when I heard nothing from you, there was no reaction in court here, I didn't bother to ask President Meron but I took it for granted that the permission or permit had been communicated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Many people have been working on it, Your Honour. There just wasn't much to tell you except that we were still working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do also want to say publicly that I do appreciate the fact that in spite of the fact that you did not receive any communication, you continued to show up here and carry on with your duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the reason we picked Wednesday yesterday was we wanted to be sure that any witnesses who had come from out of town would be finished before we took that position. The remaining witnesses this week -- the witness this week is from the Prosecutor's Office, so it wouldn't be a big inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, can you bring Mr. Brown on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could but in fact we -- counsel are saying a very firm no. Your Honour, we can't get the next witness up here until Monday in any event so that there is a witness -- the only -- the witness who is coming today is the only witness dealing with the events of Sipovo which you're going to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The military expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we put him down for two days, so if he testifies Thursday and Friday he'll be finished definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know why we need two days for him but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I actually think Your Honours will find that, rather like Mr. Treanor, his evidence is such as to explain quite a lot of what happened. I know he's already testified in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I have read his evidence in Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, but that only dealt with one aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also read the testimony of the counterpart.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, the general that was called in Stakic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, unless Mr. Ackerman is calling him, that evidence is -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's partly confirmative, partly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we are perfectly happy -- Mr. Koumjian who dealt with it says we are perfectly happy for the transcript to be put into evidence of the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Partly -- to a large extent he confirmed the testimony of Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then he disagrees substantially on other matters too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, problem is I'm not sure Your Honour ought to have read it because it's not evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. But I am -- before hearing the evidence of Mr. Brown, I thought I better read the -- we are talking of experts after all. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I mean, I don't think I'm going to take the point, Your Honour, but technically, it's -- I hope Your Honour was reading it as light reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reading it as I read other books about Bosnia, about what happened in the area. I'm not deciding the case on what witnesses may have said in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And Your Honour will notice that Mr. Koumjian did cross-examine him on some of the things that he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's up -- I would expect Mr. Ackerman to bring an expert himself on this matter because it's an important aspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's right. That's why we put him down for two days and the documents we think will be easier to look at because they are going to be in sanction, so you can put them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's start with this witness. I think we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour excuse me as well from the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to be excused and I will leave you all in the very capable hands of Madam Baruch and I'll go do some very interesting things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You're welcome, Mr. Ackerman. And let's hope that by tomorrow you get this permit. Things move slowly but at the end, most of the time, they do move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, see you when the next witness is called. I'll be back for the next witness. I believe he'll be ready today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You told me yesterday that this was going to be a very short --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think Ms. Richterova says the direct will be about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Most probably, but you know me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And since I know you I am going to make sure that you finish -- let's see how you get along. And then, Mrs. Baruch, how long do you expect your cross-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I have to say, Your Honour, that because we refer to these witnesses only by pseudonym, I'm not even sure which of the two witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 105, the Sipovo --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: The Sipovo witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, yes. I suppose it will be a very short cross-examination because it's -- there is very little to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: If you recall, the first day that I started somebody asked how long is my cross-examination and I gave something like 26 pages; today I have five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I would expect it to be a very short cross-examination to tell you the truth, because there isn't much you can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cross-examine about. Madam Richterova, did you discuss with Mr. Koumjian how much he requires with the next -- with the following witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To be honest, I didn't discuss it with him, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But because he can testify until tomorrow so there won't be any problem, but I don't think that he's a very long witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. 7.223 the next one after this one, Ms. Gustin?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, this witness, 7.223, is the witness who was injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Injured. So who is the next one after 105?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Ms. Gustin will tell me in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I'm getting confused honestly now with the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The next witness will be 7.277, which is BT99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 99. That's another intercept, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness, Mrs. Baruch, will be 7.277. Is it your witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: 7.277 is one that I was expecting to take, but you said a different number for the next witness, and I have been preparing for Witness number 7.124 from Sipovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's my witness who will testify right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And it's BT105.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can leave the curtains down, no? So that members of the public will not be able to look -- what seems to have happened -- they have found it, all right. They have found it. I was going to suggest that -- thank you, usher. So let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. I saw you nodding, so I take it that you are receiving interpretation in your language? And therefore you can follow what I am saying? Good. You are about to start giving evidence in this trial, which has been going on against Radoslav Brdjanin, and before you do so, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration which is contained in the piece of paper that you have just been handed. Basically it's equivalent to an oath. Namely that in the course of your testimony, you undertake, you promise, that you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a chair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You asked or the Prosecution asked on your behalf that for some protective measures to hide your identity. We have decided, Judges Janu and Judge Taya and myself to grant you the protective measures that the Prosecution has asked for you, namely that you will not be referred to by your name but you will be referred to by a number, which we have given you, and you in fact you are going to be referred to as Witness BT105. And we also have consented, granted, that no one will be able to see your face outside these -- this courtroom, since that we have placed an order that there will be visual distortion. If you look at your screen, at the monitor in front of you, that is how others are going to see you. In other words, no one will be able to see your face directly or be able to recognise you through your face. Otherwise, the testimony will be given in an open session and any parts during the testimony which may reveal your identity will be heard in private session so that no one can hear them. For example, very soon you're going to be shown a piece of paper with your name. You will not read it. You will -- out aloud, you will just look at it and say yes, this is my name. When you're giving testimony you're not going to give any indications of any relatives, et cetera, in open session because otherwise people can identify you so you need to help us so that we try and do our best to continue hiding your identity. And when it is necessary we will go into private session. Please have a look at that piece of paper and tell me whether that is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Baruch would like to see it. That's going to be, Ms. Richterova, an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2412 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it's under seal. We go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I can start in open session and then we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever you tell me, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to start with some background information about the Sipovo municipality and I want to show the witness a map of ethnic composition, and we will distribute the spare copies to Your Honours as well and to the Defence, of course. Maybe if we could place it on the ELMO it would be easier. Examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see the map of ethnic distribution in the Sipovo municipality. At the same time, at the beginning, I would like to read one small part from the exhibit P2402. At this moment, we don't need to show this document to the witness because I only want him to confirm whether -- whether the numbers -- whether the figures are correct. This document states that according to the 1991 census, the municipality numbered about 15.500 inhabitants. Of those, 12.317 or 79.20 per cent were Serbs, and 2.990 or 19.27 per cent were Muslims. Is it correct, this ethnic distribution, for the municipality of Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I think that it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you -- if you are so kind and have a look at the map of Sipovo, can you tell us whether, according to this map, the distribution is correct or whether you want to point some errors? And if you want to point at the map, you have to do it at the ELMO, at the machine, not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: All right. The village of Lubovo was mostly populated by Muslims. They had majority there. The same applies to the village of Vrazic. In the suburb and settlement of Sarici, there were a lot of Muslims living there. The same goes for Cifluk. In Sipovo itself, a large number of Muslims lived. The village of Brdjani, Majevac, and Donji Mujdzici. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A minute ago, I read from the Exhibit P2402 and it says that the municipality was divided into seven local communes of Mirisna [phoen], Vajenica [phoen]. It was Sipovo town, if you could just point at -- we can see it, Volari was another local commune, we can see it. The other one was Pljeva, which -- we cannot see the word "Pljeva." Can you show us where Pljeva is and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Pljeva covers Dragnic, Majevac, and Brdjani. It encompasses those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Pljeva was predominantly occupied by which people -- which people, which nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: It was mixed. I'm not sure of percentages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we have Mirisna, Vajenica, Strojica. Can you show us Mirisna, Vajenica, Strojica, where it is? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: The local community Stojica includes settlements along the valley of the Jana river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic composition of these villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: They were Serb villages. That was their ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also true for the local communes of Babici, Grbavica, and Pribeljci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you show us which direction on this map is the municipality of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it means that the municipality Jajce borders with predominantly Muslim villages in the municipality of Sipovo. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. Duljci and Volari [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go now into private session for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session Madam Registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (Redacted) (Redacted) 2 3

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm done with the map and I should tender it under Exhibit Number P2413.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to talk to you briefly about the life in the Sipovo municipality and Sipovo town. How would you describe the atmosphere in the municipality itself, during the year 1992? First, did you notice that -- did you notice that there would be presence of military or police forces which weren't present there before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us more about this. What -- if you say -- because you are saying yes, what did you notice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I noticed police wearing camouflage military uniform; those were the so-called Martic's men. So these policemen moved about the town with automatic weapons in large groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any members of the Martic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I did. [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These two men, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we redact this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to. This is what I mean, you have to be careful because we try to protect you and then you don't protect yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the presence of Martic's group. Can you tell us generally how the life changed in Sipovo? Were they -- were there more shootings than before? Were there some explosions? Please elaborate how the life changed in Sipovo in the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I object to places other than in the village or places -- his village, or in places where he was. Because from this map, especially, Exhibit 2413, it looks to me like this would be quite a big place, and of course at the time the witness was quite young and so I think it would be purely speculative for him to think about other areas in which he did not live or associate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he is aware of what the situation was in other places, he can testify. For example, if you read his statement of the 3rd of June of 1997, he explains what he saw one day in July and August of 1991, when he was on holiday in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, there was a big mistake. You probably received a statement of another person. Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's -- yeah, let's go into private Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position as far as I'm concerned, just to make it clear, the witness can be asked and he is expected to answer any questions about events taking place outside of Sipovo if he knows about them. Especially if he has witnessed them himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before this long exchange of our opinions, I will repeat for you the question: Can you please describe briefly the atmosphere in the municipality of Sipovo, as you know it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: In March and April of 1992, the said armed forces appeared in Sipovo. Their presence was obvious everywhere around the town and surrounding villages. Their conduct -- first of all, let me say that they were armed with firearms, they frequently consumed alcohol, and they fired from their weapons while under the influence of alcohol. And that was particularly widespread in the evening hours and during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you still remember their uniforms? You mentioned that they were in camouflage uniforms but did you notice any particular insignias on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the national emblem with a two-headed eagle. That's a Serb national emblem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that they were shooting and mainly they were shooting in the evenings. Did they -- did you witness or did you hear anything about damage of particular properties? And I am again talking about the year, end of 1991, first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Again, I have to object, the witness said in March of 1992 these people came. So the end of 1991 and three months at least --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I apologise but when I said -- I'm referring generally to the situation in Sipovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead and please answer the question. It doesn't make a difference, Mrs. Baruch, the way it has been framed now, we have seen the context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at the period of time that there were some houses, some premises, destroyed or damaged in the Sipovo municipality, as again, as you know -- if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I would say that the damage occurred a bit later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "a bit later," when did it start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: It started sometime after May, meaning in June and onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When talking about this atmosphere, can you tell us whether you noticed that a checkpoint or checkpoints would be set up, either in the town of Sipovo or in other places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that. The checkpoints were there in late March and on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us where exactly these checkpoints were located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Initially, the checkpoints were located on the road leading to Jajce. Later on, they were set up in other sites which were on the exit from the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these checkpoints were set up in late March. In late March, was it difficult to pass these checkpoints, to pass through these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Initially, the control wasn't rigorous, but later on it was more intense. All of the passers-by, especially Muslims, were searched and some people were abused physically and verbally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, when you said "later on," can you tell us what period of time you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: From early June, let's say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question about the checkpoints: Do you remember who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: The forces that I've mentioned in the beginning, Martic's men and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the end of the sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the last part of your answer. They only got as far as the forces that I have mentioned at the beginning, Martic's men, and then you said something else but they couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Whenever it's convenient for you -- I mean you've got another two minutes, three minutes --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In fact, I just wanted to ask you if we can break now because it's a convenient time for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I can tell you this: There is a wrong date of birth also in another statement that you gave us. Yes. It's not that I am keen on apologies. I don't care but we need to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we try to conclude in half an hour, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian is very anxious to start with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before I start talking about documents, I have one last question about the general atmosphere in Sipovo municipality. To your knowledge, during the first half of the year 1992, or the end of 1991, did you witness or did you hear about any murders which would be committed in the municipality of Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I heard about the murder of Mehemed Ganibegovic. Also I heard about the disappearance of Mersih Kudic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't witness these murders, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't witness that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear who supposedly committed these crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that this was committed by Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown the Exhibit P2395?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In B/C/S, I want to refer to the page with -- which bears the ERN Number 0219-4135. And in English version, it is the second page, right below the word "item 2." It says, under item 2 -- first, I'm sorry, I will start with the document itself. This document is dated 19 of May, 1992, and these are minutes of the Sipovo municipal Crisis Staff meeting. My first question is: Did you know that there was a Crisis Staff in Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second question is: Did you know who was the President of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I believe it was Dragan Djukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do so, Dragan and Rade Djukic would be the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read under the item 2 a few parts. It's Jovo Bogdanovic said that we had searched the houses in Besnjevo, and it refers to disarmament. Nedjo Gvozden says: "Until we resolve the matter of disarming the Muslims in Sipovo, we should talk with prominent Muslims, the units will impose a blockade on Sipovo, and start searching houses. And Rade Dj: The batillion will not begin operations towards Jajce until the disarmament of the Muslims is finished." My first question is: Did you hear any announcements with respect to handing over illegal or legal weapons in Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any public announcements, but I am aware of the fact that the police did take all the legal weapons. For example, my father's hunting rifle was taken away from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether your father was the only person, or whether the weapons were taken from other people, and you can probably talk about the people in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I know that weapons were confiscated from all the Muslims in my village, and I also heard that the same happened everywhere on the territory of the municipality. Only those Muslims who accepted to be members of the armed Serbian forces could keep their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took these weapons? Was it members of army or the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Those were regular policemen and the confiscation of the weapons was accompanied by issuing certificates for the arms taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of the page in which we read about the disarmament in B/C/S version, 0219-4135, is Spiro, the Muslims were buying weapons. Did you know anything about the fact that Muslims were generally buying weapons, either legally or illegally? And I'm again referring towards the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is another conclusion, and it is on the page 4, and in B/C/S version, it is on the page 0219-4136, and it says: Disarmament of paramilitary units and Muslims by 24 hours on 22nd of May, 1992. Now I would like to turn into another subject, which was discussed during this meeting but I will go back to one more thing. Do you know whether, when you had to hand over your weapons, whether the houses were searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I don't remember. In any case, this didn't happen to my family. And as for others, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The other issue which I want to discuss is the issue which is mentioned in B/C/S on the page 0219-4139, and it is on the bottom of this page. Did you find it? And it is page 6 on the bottom. It says: "Firing Muslims from specific positions, change in the post office, change in the fire-fighting society, change at the petrol station." Did you know anything that Muslims in some positions were dismissed or were replaced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that. I am only aware of the cases of companies going bankrupt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown -- I'm done with this exhibit. Can the witness be shown Exhibit 2398.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I will talk about the issue which is mentioned in B/C/S version on the page 0219-4122, and English version, it is page 3 at the bottom. The first thing is mentioned: "Milorad G., take a stand with regard to the Muslims?" And Savo Popovic talks: "As for the Muslims, a public announcement should be made if we are going to expel them. Families of those who refuse to the call-up should be told to leave." Did you -- and now I'm again talking about the year -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I see Ms. Baruch --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Madam Baruch. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't find -- we just got the exhibit numbers today and I have to find the number that corresponds with 2398. Are you still on 2398?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I can provide you with extra copies for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think I found it. I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is document dated 2nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, both of you. Let's proceed. It's page 3 at the bottom of the page that you need to refer, Mrs. Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Just to be certain about this, this is an unsigned and unsealed document. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about that because at the end of the day, we will go through all this and we will take into consideration the general objection that was made earlier, at the early stages of the trial. So you doesn't need to stand up and remind us that this has been objected to because we have -- every document is recorded as having been objected to or not objected to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear during the year 1992 any announcement which would allowing Muslims to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it difficult to leave the municipality of Sipovo during the year of 1992? And I am referring to Muslims or to non-Serbs living in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I know that in the first half of 1991 [as interpreted], some Muslims left Sipovo and went in the direction of Jajce. After that, it became impossible to leave Sipovo. You couldn't go anywhere. Up to 12 February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the transcript, we have, in the first half of the year 1991. Did you say that the Muslims were able to leave in the first half of the year 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I meant 1992, and I believe that this is what I said also.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I am done with this document. Can the witness be shown Exhibit P2399. It is -- these are minutes from the session of the Crisis Staff held on 4th June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will start with the page number 1, and in B/C/S, it is middle of the second page, page 0219-4125, in the middle, and it says: "Stojica received 50 rifles, Babici, lack of weapons." At the beginning we were talking about the villages, which villages were predominantly Muslim villages, which were predominantly Serbs. Stojica and Babici are villages in the Sipovo municipality. Who were the people who lived there, which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Serbs. There were no Muslims in those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- because we were already talking about the Muslims who had to hand over their weapons. Did you know whether Serbs first owned weapons and whether they had to hand them over as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I am not aware of the fact that they were supposed to hand over their weapons, and I'm aware that others did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Serbs wearing -- carrying, I'm sorry -- carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they -- those Serbs who carried these weapons, were they soldiers, policemen, or civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: All those that you mentioned were there. There were policemen, there were soldiers, there were civilians. Very often they were minors. In other words, people who were not trained to use those weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want to direct your attention to the page in B/C/S, 0219-4129, and in English, it is page 3, in the middle, right above the item 3. Spiro S. says: "I would appreciate being given the paper that says that the work obligation applies to the Muslims who are loyal." And then again we have: "A public announcement should be made that any Muslim who wants to leave can do it safely." We already heard your comment on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Ms. Richterova, your previous question was different because his -- the record in the minutes was different. You're referring to 2398, no? The previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the previous statement, on page 3, Savo Popovic is reported to have stated: "As for Muslims, a public announcement should be made if we are going to expel them. Families of those who refused the call-up should be told to leave." And he said he had not heard any such announcement. This is a little bit -- not a little bit, it's dramatically different. A public announcement should be made that any Muslim who wants to leave can do it safely. So go straight to this and ask him whether he ever heard such an announcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No need to apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear any public announcement that Muslims can leave the municipality if they wanted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to direct your attention to the word -- the work obligation. Was there a work obligation in the municipality of Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes, there was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: -- work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did it start, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I can't remember the date but I believe that it was in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This works obligation, was it for all the people or just for some ethnicity living in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: The work obligation applied to Muslims, to the able-bodied Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in the work obligation or did anyone from your family participate in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I did not participate in the work obligation, but my father and my brother did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from them what they were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we remain in open session now or go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can remain in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard from them that they did menial jobs. They were digging trenches and they worked on other features on the front line. When there was no such work, then they did various jobs in agriculture, jobs that had to do with cattle raising. All this was happening in the territory of Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm done with this document. Can the witness be shown Exhibit P2401? It is document dated 8 of August, 1992. It is from the 1st Krajina Brigade command, Sipovo command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the middle, we can read, "The mosques in Besnjevo, Sipovo, and Pljeva were bombed and destroyed at 21st hours, 23rd hours, and 2 hours respectively on 7 August, 1992." Do you remember the fact that the mosques were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I remember. I heard, and I felt, the explosion before the mosque in Pljeva was destroyed. However, I didn't see who did that. I only know the outcome, the results, on the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe very briefly how these mosques were destroyed. What happened to the minaret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: The mosques were completely destroyed, including the minarets. Many tombstones which are in the vicinity of the mosques were also damaged. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm done with this document. Can the witness be shown Exhibit 2402? It is a document with the title: "Assessment of the Security Situation in Sipovo Municipality." And it is not dated. Ms. Baruch, do you have this? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to the page B006-8776, which is the second page in B/C/S, and also second page in English. Can you please have a look at the second paragraph from the bottom. You had the opportunity to read this document before, when I showed you it. And it says, among others, "Enemy activities against the Serbian people and its republic were orchestrated by extremists from the Party of Democratic Action who were the leaders of the Muslim people in the municipality. The most extreme among them were," and there is the list of people. First, you can see the list of the people mentioned in this document. Did you know any one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. I knew some of them, including Sakib Ribic, Kadrija Cuk, Nedzad Dadovic -- and Nedzad Dadovic, Coric Dervis, Hodzic Zaim. These are the people that I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion as you knew these people, were -- did you count them as extremists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: No. I didn't consider them to be extremists, because I knew them to be leading people in our municipality in the Party of Democratic Action, which at the time was the ruling Muslim party. I believe that that was the reason they were considered to be extremist. Kadrija Cuk was a military expert and this is the reason I believe he was considered to be dangerous to the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was the President of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: The President of the SDA in Sipovo municipality was Sakib Ribic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to the page 3 in both languages, and I'm talking about the middle paragraph, the longest one, and if we go to the last two sentences, first the witness read this document, and it's talking about incidents which happened in the municipality, and these two sentences say: "Most of these crimes and misdemeanors were committed by uniformed individuals in cooperation with military organs, these persons were arrested and handed over to other organs. However, after sometime, the said individuals were released and they are again endangering the safety of persons and property." Does it reflect accurately the situation as you know and as you experienced? And please just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I have to object to that because the people aren't named. Now, I understand that he can testify from his own observations and experience, but if he does, can we please have him give the names of those people he experienced were treated that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go step by step, because I also more or less would have suggested that you read more of the paragraph that we are talking about, because first you refer to them as incidents but here we are talking about crimes and misdemeanors. So I'm taking over for a while, if you don't mind, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I appreciate it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In this paragraph, sir, and follow me in the document that you have in -- before you, which is in your own language, it states that: "Over the past few months, the public security station has been confronting major security problems. This relates primarily to a significant number of serious crimes such as murders, robberies, armed robberies, aggravated thefts, assaults on and resistance to authorised officials, threats to security, causing public danger and other crimes as well as a large number of misdemeanors, such as brawls, physical assaults on others, endangering the safety of others, obstructing and resisting police officers, and other offences endangering the safety of citizens." I'll stop here for the time being. Would you agree with what is stated in this report, that there was a significant number of such crimes and misdemeanours as I have described to you by reading from this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's move to the next part. "Most of these crimes and miss demeanors were committed by uniformed individuals." Let's stop there now. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You couldn't say. "In cooperation with military organs, these persons were arrested and handed over to other organs." Are you aware of any arrests having taken place for allegedly having committed -- of persons allegedly having committed such crimes and misdemeanors to start with? That's the first part of my question. Do you recall any arrests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And would you recall or would you agree to the statement that we have here that after being arrested, they were handed over to other organs? In other words, not processed by the public security station themselves but handed over to other organs? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the statement continues: "However, after some time the said individuals were released." Would you agree with that? Are you aware that those who were arrested were released some time after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would agree with that, because I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it continues, with the allegation that they are again endangering the safety of persons and property. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in a position to give us any names of such persons who were arrested, released, and became dangerous or a menace once more? Would you know any names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you the name of Goran Kalajdzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, Goran Kalajdzija was arrested at one point and then released? Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was arrested for murder and two attempted murders, and released some two months after his arrest. After that, he continued with his activities which endangered the security of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Does that satisfy you both, Madam Richterova and Madam Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that you went into these details. I intended to do it at a later stage but I think we saved some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you have got ten minutes less now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Because I have ten minutes less, can we go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have only two subjects which I want to cover. Can the witness be shown Exhibit P2403.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is official note Sipovo wartime department compiled on 16 September, 1992. This is extensive description of a number of incidents involving murder, arson, an explosion in Sipovo municipality over the last month and half. You had the opportunity to have a look at this document before. It talks about houses who were burned in the Sipovo municipalities and you were also talking about this in your statement. I can start: "In the municipality 20 to 30 houses were burned in the village of Besnjevo." Then it talks about -- towards the end, fire to three houses and stable of Muslim in the village of Cifluk. Do you remember that houses were set on fire in respective of villages within the municipality of Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember who were the owners of these houses and stables who were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness, you personally, any incident when you saw someone set a house or houses or stables on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I was not an eyewitness to that. However, I saw frequently the consequences of arson, or rather I saw the flames. The houses and auxiliary facilities engulfed in flames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the village of Besnjevo, which I mentioned, and Cifluk, do you remember any hamlets or villages in which the houses or stables were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. [redacted]--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, let's go into private session straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to show the witness -- I am done with this exhibit and I want to show the witness Exhibit 2406.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement and already today that you left the municipality in February, 1993. How did you leave and where did you meet to have some paperwork done to be allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: All of the documents which we were required to have, and this boils down to a voluntary relinquishment of property and the residence and we also had to have a certificate that we have paid for all of the taxes, this document had to be obtained in Sipovo municipality. Prior to our departure, we had to go to Banja Luka and we had to show all of the listed documents there in order to be able to leave in an organised convoy in the direction of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, do you remember -- do you know whom did you give these documents to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: I know that there was some agency whose name I didn't know. The lady organising the trip was called Perka. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person Perka, was she present when you -- when you boarded the buses, and did she accompany you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. She was present and she was on the buses with us, and went all the way until the separation line, which is in Travnik municipality, in a place called Turbe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is really very long, and it shows some more than 1200 names, and the family of the witness is mentioned in this document as well. There were -- were there more than one convoys in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. There were two convoys. One left on the 12th of February, and the other one on the 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P2407.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is announcement which refers to the second convoy, and we know that you already left. What I am interested in is in the statement in the first paragraph: "Citizens who have expressed a wish to move out of Sipovo municipality can travel in an organised convoy with the most necessary personal luggage." Do you still remember what you were allowed to take with you when leaving the Sipovo municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: We were allowed to take what we could carry in our hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the previous list, and all other lists which are in the Sipovo binder, it is also under Exhibit P2409, and 2410, and we do not need to show it to the witness, it says: "Lists of Muslims from the Sipovo municipality area who voluntarily applied for resettlement." Were you leaving voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment, we left voluntarily but only after all of the incidents had happened, and after we were forced to do that, because we didn't have a choice. We could not survive otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I concluded my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova. Madam Baruch, please? Cross-examined by Mrs. Baruch:

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you prefer to come forward -- it's up to you. I'm just offering you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court I'll already stand here because my stuff is already spread out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good noon, it's not yet afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have until Friday, Mrs. Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Barbara Baruch I am one of the Defence counsel in this case. You and I have not previously had a chance to speak; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have had a chance to speak with a representative of the Prosecutor's Office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Witness, my understanding is that in this jurisdiction, they call that proofing when they speak with a witness. Did anybody -- did you speak with the Prosecution shortly before coming here to testify, that is, within the last week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that with Ms. Richterova, this Prosecutor who has been questioning you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. And that was on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you make any statements on Saturday that were recorded in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I would ask on the record for such statements, but I notice that Ms. Richterova might have a response to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I can make the explanation. The witness noticed some errors which I recorded but then I went back to Rule 92 bis statement and I realised that these changes have already been done. So I of course didn't do exactly the same statement as was done before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we can proceed, Madam Baruch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when you were speaking with the Prosecution on Saturday, I think they showed you several documents that you had not previously seen before. That is some of the documents that the Prosecutor referred to today while she was questioning you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes. That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for me, it appears that those documents, at least the ones she referred to, were documents that purport to be from something called the Crisis Staff. Was that one of the documents you were -- you saw on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some minutes from what purported to be a Crisis Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to commend you for your precision in answering questions. I've noticed that you've been very honest about what you saw before and what you had not seen, and we appreciate that. I'm sure if you were on trial, or I was on trial, we would appreciate that. Now, you said you had never heard of a Crisis Staff before, and I assume it was before looking at those documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So anything you know about those documents come purely from the documents themselves that had been shown to you; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you ended -- Ms. Richterova ended her questioning of you with regard to your leaving the area of Sipovo. Did you, before you left Sipovo, notice that there were many Serbs, Serb refugees, coming into Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't notice stranger -- people you had never seen before, perhaps even living in Muslim homes that were not in use? You never saw that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT105
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this gets too definite so perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session. Whenever you think we should, Mrs. Baruch, just give me a hint and we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of July, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
